subject: INLA crashing on large-scale binomial model

messages.author: 722c8c333c4ea333
messages.subject: INLA crashing on large-scale binomial model
parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to run a relatively simple model and getting a segmentation fault error before the hyperparameter optimization stage. The model is logistic regression model with a fixed precision matrix for the regression coefficients. With a design matrix of 600,000 x 50, INLA crashes, however at a smaller size of 60,000 x 50, there are no errors.

I'm using an AWS EC2 instance running an ubuntu AMI; in particular, memory and other resources should not be a bottleneck (this code fails on an instance with 120G memory and 20G free in disk storage). Below is the session info, and I've attached code for a minimal working example that replicates the error I see with my real data, along with the verbose output.

Thanks for your help!
Dan

thanks for your example. this is 'to large model' problem, and is why
it crash.

due to the internal design, this is exactly the type of model INLA does
not do well computationally. since the internal latent field includes
also the linear predictor, then the internal size is n+p (or 2*n+p, in
the first case), and this is why there are problems. the reason for
this choice, it that other tasks are then easier.

since you do not have any 'random effects', then the output of glm()
would be more or less the same as with INLA, since the priors will be
neglible compared to the data.

I attach an edited version of your code, which I think is what you
ment. btw, the results in the two versions are not the same, couldn't
easily find out why, but I guess you can.

Best
H

messages.author: 722c8c333c4ea333
messages.subject: Re: INLA crashing on large-scale binomial model
parts:
Thanks for the info, Havard. With the simulated data example here, glm() indeed would indeed provide an acceptable solution. However the actual data set and model I am working with includes additional latent terms that are very well suited for INLA and not easily implemented with another software package. 

The fact that INLA is not computationally efficient for a large n model is not that much of a concern for me as long as I can get inference to run successfully, as I have no problem using large-resource instances on AWS. Is the large n failure something for which there is a known workaround or cause of the error? 

Also, by the way in case anyone is interested, the reason the results are a bit different for the two versions of the example code is because only one model has a diagonal term in the latent field... my apologies for the sloppiness there!

Thanks,
Dan
